Operating in an unstable, septic patient carries high mortality. Delaying drainage for days allows progression to shock. Imaging and discharge ignore the emergency, and cholecystectomy follows once he recovers.

items.stem: Minutes after a brachial plexus block with a long-acting local anesthetic, a 47-year-old man reports tinnitus and a metallic taste, then has a generalized seizure followed by wide-complex bradycardia. What is the most specific treatment to give along with airway support?
options: Intravenous lipid emulsion
Intravenous epinephrine at full dose and nothing else
Intravenous calcium chloride
Intravenous atropine as the only agent
items.explanation: Perioral symptoms, seizure, and cardiovascular collapse soon after injection of a local anesthetic indicate systemic toxicity. Along with airway control, seizure suppression with a benzodiazepine, and basic life support, intravenous lipid emulsion binds the drug and is the specific antidote. Full-dose epinephrine can worsen arrhythmias, so reduced doses are advised. Calcium does not reverse the sodium channel blockade. Atropine alone does not correct the cardiotoxicity.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has a clinically node-negative 2.5-cm estrogen receptor positive, HER2 negative invasive breast cancer. She chooses lumpectomy with sentinel node biopsy, which shows two positive nodes with no extranodal extension. She will receive whole-breast radiation and endocrine therapy. What is the best management of the axilla?
options: Completion axillary dissection
Repeat sentinel mapping in six weeks
Mastectomy to allow full nodal assessment
No further axillary surgery
items.explanation: In women with T1 or T2, clinically node-negative disease who have one or two positive sentinel nodes, undergo lumpectomy, and receive whole-breast radiation, completion axillary dissection does not improve survival or regional control. Dissection adds lymphedema and numbness. Repeat mapping has no role. Mastectomy offers no survival advantage and is unnecessary. Systemic therapy is planned from the tumor biology and nodal findings.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has a 1.5-cm biopsy-proven infiltrative (morpheaform) basal cell carcinoma of the nasal tip. What is the preferred treatment?
options: Standard excision with a 2-mm margin
Mohs micrographic surgery
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen
Topical imiquimod cream for several weeks
items.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma in a high-risk site such as the central face, or with infiltrative histology, has a high recurrence rate after standard excision, and tissue sparing matters on the nose. Mohs surgery gives the highest cure rate with maximal preservation through complete margin examination. A narrow standard margin risks positive margins. Cryotherapy and topical agents suit small, superficial, low-risk lesions and do not control deep infiltrative disease.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man falls from a ladder. Blood pressure is 78/50 mm Hg, and the pelvis is mechanically unstable. A focused ultrasound examination of the abdomen is negative, and a pelvic binder is in place. After two units of blood his pressure remains low. What is the best next step?
options: Exploratory laparotomy to search for an abdominal source
External fixation of the pelvis as the only intervention
Preperitoneal pelvic packing or angiographic embolization with ongoing transfusion
Removal of the binder and repeat examination in the ward
items.explanation: Persistent shock with an unstable pelvic ring and a negative abdominal ultrasound points to pelvic hemorrhage, usually venous or from small arterial branches. Preperitoneal packing or angiographic embolization, combined with balanced transfusion, controls it. Laparotomy is not supported by a negative examination and releases tamponade. External fixation stabilizes bone but does not stop bleeding alone. Removing the binder worsens volume loss in a patient who is already unstable.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has tachycardia of 125, fever, and left upper quadrant pain on postoperative day 3 after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. He is hemodynamically stable with a soft abdomen and rising white count. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Computed tomography of the abdomen with water-soluble oral contrast
Observation with antipyretics and repeat examination tomorrow
Barium upper gastrointestinal series
Discharge with oral antibiotics and early follow-up
items.explanation: Unexplained tachycardia, fever, and upper abdominal pain early after sleeve gastrectomy suggest a staple line leak until proven otherwise, and tachycardia is its most sensitive sign. A stable patient is evaluated with contrast computed tomography to detect collections and extravasation. An unstable patient would go directly to the operating room. Waiting allows sepsis to advance. Barium is a poor choice if perforation is possible. Discharge risks a missed leak.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man on postoperative day 5 after low anterior resection has fever, a heart rate of 128, and diffuse abdominal rigidity. Blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg, white count is elevated, and computed tomography shows free fluid and air with an anastomotic defect. What is the best management?
options: Percutaneous drainage alone with intravenous antibiotics
Broad-spectrum antibiotics and close observation in the intensive care unit
Rectal contrast study to grade the leak before any decision
Reoperation with washout, takedown of the anastomosis, and end colostomy
items.explanation: Anastomotic leak with generalized peritonitis and early shock requires prompt reoperation to control contamination. In an unstable or septic patient, the safest procedure is usually washout, takedown of the anastomosis, and an end colostomy. Percutaneous drainage suits a contained, localized collection in a stable patient. Antibiotics alone cannot control diffuse peritonitis. Further contrast studies delay source control without changing the need for surgery.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis has a solitary 3-cm hepatocellular carcinoma. He is Child-Pugh class A with normal bilirubin and platelet count, and he has no varices or ascites. Hepatic venous pressure measurement is not elevated. What is the preferred treatment?
options: Systemic sorafenib therapy
Transarterial chemoembolization alone
Hepatic resection
Transplant evaluation as the only option
items.explanation: A single early hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient with preserved liver function and no clinically significant portal hypertension is best treated by resection, which offers good long-term survival. Systemic therapy is for advanced disease. Chemoembolization is used for intermediate-stage disease or as a bridge. Transplantation is an excellent option when portal hypertension or poor function make resection unsafe, but it is not the only choice in this well-compensated patient.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a 4.5-cm adrenal mass found incidentally during imaging for kidney stones. The unenhanced attenuation is 40 Hounsfield units. She has hypertension and no other symptoms. What should be done before any intervention?
options: Percutaneous needle biopsy of the mass
Biochemical testing for autonomous cortisol secretion and pheochromocytoma
Immediate laparoscopic adrenalectomy without testing
Repeat imaging in three years with no hormonal evaluation or biopsy planned
items.explanation: An adrenal incidentaloma needs hormonal evaluation: a dexamethasone suppression test for cortisol, plasma or urinary metanephrines to exclude pheochromocytoma, and aldosterone with renin when hypertension is present. An undiagnosed pheochromocytoma can cause hypertensive crisis during biopsy or surgery. Biopsy is rarely informative and is dangerous before exclusion. Operating without testing risks adrenal crisis or catecholamine surge. A lesion this size with indeterminate density warrants active evaluation.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with aspiration pneumonia has severe acute respiratory distress syndrome with a ratio of arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen of 120. Which ventilator strategy is most strongly supported to reduce mortality?
options: Tidal volume of 6 mL per kilogram of predicted weight, plateau pressure below 30 cm of water
Tidal volume of 10 to 12 mL per kilogram of actual body weight to normalize carbon dioxide levels
Routine high-dose corticosteroids at the start of ventilation
Inhaled nitric oxide as standard first-line therapy
items.explanation: Lung-protective ventilation with a low tidal volume based on predicted body weight and limited plateau pressure reduces ventilator-induced injury and mortality in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Permissive hypercapnia is accepted. Large tidal volumes overdistend aerated lung. Routine steroids have not shown consistent benefit. Inhaled nitric oxide improves oxygenation briefly but has not improved survival, so it serves only as rescue therapy.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man has a distal esophageal adenocarcinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound shows invasion of the adventitia with two abnormal periesophageal nodes, and positron emission tomography shows no distant disease. What is the most appropriate treatment plan?
options: Upfront esophagectomy without further treatment
Endoscopic mucosal resection alone
Neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by esophagectomy
Palliative stent placement and supportive care
items.explanation: Locally advanced, resectable esophageal adenocarcinoma, meaning tumor beyond the muscularis or node-positive without distant spread, is treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiation or perioperative chemotherapy before esophagectomy, which improves survival over surgery alone. Endoscopic resection is limited to superficial disease. Palliative stenting is for unresectable or metastatic disease. Upfront surgery gives inferior results in tumors of this stage.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has left lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Computed tomography shows sigmoid diverticulitis with a 6-cm pericolic abscess and no free air. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Emergency sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy and Hartmann closure later
Percutaneous image-guided drainage with intravenous antibiotics
Oral antibiotics alone as an outpatient
Colonoscopy within the next day to rule out cancer
items.explanation: A diverticular abscess larger than about 3 to 4 cm in a stable patient is managed with percutaneous drainage and antibiotics, which often avoids an emergency operation and allows elective resection later if indicated. Emergency colectomy is for peritonitis or failure of drainage. Oral antibiotics alone do not clear a large abscess. Colonoscopy during acute inflammation risks perforation and is deferred for several weeks.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman is hemodynamically stable after a motor vehicle collision. Computed tomography shows a grade III splenic laceration with a contrast blush and a moderate amount of free fluid. Hemoglobin is stable. What is the best management?
options: Splenic artery angioembolization with close monitoring
Immediate splenectomy
Bed rest and observation with no intervention
Laparoscopic splenorrhaphy tonight
items.explanation: A stable patient with a contrast blush after splenic injury has active bleeding that carries a high risk of failed observation. Angioembolization controls it and preserves the spleen, avoiding lifelong infection risk. Splenectomy is reserved for instability or failed embolization. Observation alone is appropriate when there is no blush and the patient is stable. Splenorrhaphy is rarely performed laparoscopically in trauma and needs conditions that do not apply here.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man is struck by a baseball and is briefly unconscious, then talks normally. Two hours later he becomes drowsy and develops a dilated right pupil. Head computed tomography shows a lens-shaped hyperdense collection with midline shift. What is the best management?
options: Repeat head computed tomography in 24 hours
Hypertonic saline alone with observation
Prophylactic anticonvulsant and discharge with instructions
Emergent craniotomy and evacuation of the hematoma
items.explanation: A lucid interval followed by decline, a lens-shaped collection, and herniation signs describe an epidural hematoma from a torn middle meningeal artery. Outcomes are excellent when the clot is evacuated promptly. Waiting for repeat imaging risks herniation and death. Hyperosmolar therapy can temporize but does not remove the mass. Seizure prophylaxis and discharge ignore an expanding lesion that needs surgery.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man had endoscopic clipping and epinephrine injection for a bleeding duodenal ulcer, followed by proton pump inhibitor therapy. Thirty-six hours later he vomits blood and becomes hypotensive, then responds to resuscitation. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate laparotomy and oversewing of the bleeding ulcer base
Continued intravenous proton pump inhibitor alone
Repeat endoscopy with a second attempt at hemostasis
Angiography as the first intervention
items.explanation: Rebleeding after successful initial endoscopic therapy is managed by repeat endoscopy, which controls the bleeding in most patients and spares them surgery. Embolization or surgery is considered if repeat endoscopic therapy fails. Operating at once exposes a patient to higher morbidity than a second endoscopy. Acid suppression alone does not stop active arterial bleeding. Angiography is a rescue option after endoscopic failure, not a first step.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man has a mid-rectal adenocarcinoma 6 cm from the anal verge. Pelvic MRI shows invasion through the muscularis propria with a threatened mesorectal fascia and several suspicious mesorectal nodes. Staging for distant disease is negative. What is the best treatment strategy?
options: Upfront low anterior resection followed by adjuvant therapy
Transanal local excision alone
Immediate abdominoperineal resection with no preoperative treatment
Total neoadjuvant therapy before total mesorectal excision
items.explanation: Locally advanced rectal cancer, meaning tumor beyond the muscularis, node-positive, or threatening the mesorectal fascia, is treated before surgery with chemoradiation or total neoadjuvant therapy, which lowers local recurrence and can improve sphincter preservation. Upfront surgery risks a positive circumferential margin. Local excision suits only small, early, node-negative tumors. Abdominoperineal resection is not required at 6 cm and is reserved for tumors involving the sphincter complex.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman has a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones. Final pathology reveals adenocarcinoma invading the perimuscular connective tissue, with a negative cystic duct margin. Imaging shows no distant disease. What is the best management?
options: Re-resection with liver wedge and portal lymphadenectomy
Observation with surveillance imaging alone
Adjuvant radiation to the gallbladder fossa only
Repeat simple cholecystectomy with removal of the cystic duct remnant
items.explanation: Incidental gallbladder cancer that invades beyond the muscularis is T2 or higher, and re-resection with liver resection of the gallbladder bed and regional lymphadenectomy improves survival. Simple cholecystectomy is adequate only for tumors confined to the mucosa or lamina propria. Surveillance leaves residual disease. Radiation alone cannot replace resection. Port-site excision is considered selectively, and residual disease at the cystic duct margin would add bile duct resection.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman is admitted with mild acute pancreatitis caused by gallstones. Her pain resolves, she tolerates a regular diet by day 3, and bilirubin and liver enzymes are normalizing. What is the best timing for definitive treatment of her gallstones?
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy about six weeks later
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission
Routine endoscopic sphincterotomy and no cholecystectomy
Oral ursodiol for six months and reassess
items.explanation: After mild gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy during the index admission reduces recurrent pancreatitis, readmission, and gallbladder events compared with delay. Waiting weeks exposes the patient to recurrent attacks. Sphincterotomy lowers the risk of pancreatitis but does not treat gallbladder disease. Dissolution therapy is slow and unreliable. Necrotizing or severe disease is the setting where operation is delayed until collections resolve.
